article.title: Climate Revolution
article.author: Marcus Baram
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Almost no one ran on climate change this fall, but the election may reshape climate policy all the same. Democrats won both houses of Congress, a majority of governorships and — as projected by the National Conference of State Legislatures — control of 25 state legislatures by talking about prices: gasoline, diesel, home heating and above all — electricity. Geoff Garin, a Democratic pollster who works with the advocacy group Climate Power, told Capital & Main that nearly three-quarters of Democratic candidates in battleground-state races ran at least one ad about energy costs. “The old Republican mantras of ‘drill, baby, drill’ and American energy dominance were and are wholly irrelevant to the current energy debate,” Garin said. “Instead, the energy debate now is focused on [President Donald] Trump’s ill-conceived war, on data centers, on price gouging by oil companies and on Trump’s war on clean energy.” Indeed, in a NBC News exit poll , 74% of voters pointed to the war in Iran as a major factor in their vote and 86% said they were concerned about utility costs. In Garin’s polling , 53% said producing more wind and solar power would make energy more affordable — with one in five saying renewables would make it much more affordable. Voters who rank climate first in their priorities, meanwhile, showed up early. Across the 21 states where the nonprofit Environmental Voter Project works, 49.3% of its identified climate voters cast early ballots, said Nathaniel Stinnett, the group’s founder. That was up from 41% in the 2024 presidential election and 32.5% in the 2022 midterms, he told Capital & Main. “Even if politicians weren’t talking about climate, climate voters were sure thinking about politics, because they ran to the polls to vote as soon as possible,” Stinnett said. “I think we can safely say that the climate crisis is already impacting our political choices and behavior in a profound way.” In Washington, the answer over the next two years is oversight and leverage but little new law. In state capitals and town halls, it could be a great deal more. Washington: Subpoenas, spending and one live bill Neither Democratic majority approaches the two-thirds needed to override a veto, and Trump has promised to use his freely. David Victor, a professor of public policy at the University of California, San Diego, predicted a stalemate at the federal level. That leaves three tools. The first is the gavel. Starting in January, Democratic chairs in the House reportedly plan to use subpoena power to investigate budget cuts, staff reductions and pollution-limit reversals at the Environmental Protection Agency under Administrator Lee Zeldin. They also plan to examine deals in which energy companies traded offshore wind leases for fossil fuel development or won exemptions from Clean Air Act requirements. Related: Russell Vought's Federal Grant Plan Raises Questions About Executive Power The second is the purse. Democrats intend to use must-pass spending bills — broad budget bills required to finance federal agencies, military operations, national parks and public services — to restore money for climate research, disaster resilience and clean energy grants. They also may try to revive clean energy tax credits repealed in the 2025 reconciliation law, framing them as a way to cut utility bills. A Senate majority can also block nominees to the EPA, the Energy Department and the federal bench. The third is the one major bill that’s actually already moving. The Senate voted 73-25 on Nov. 9 to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, designed to speed reviews of power plants, transmission lines and data centers. Democrats are split. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, voted no, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has voiced his opposition. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), in line to chair the House Committee on Natural Resources, wants amendments that would shield clean energy projects from agency discrimination, end federal buyouts of offshore wind leases and make data centers pay for their own power needs. “Voters sent a clear message last week that they want better deals than the ones they’ve gotten under unified Republican leadership,” said Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), a member of the environment committee who won reelection in the midterms. Democrats, he said, owe voters a deal “that delivers clean energy megawatts and jobs, near- and long-term savings on energy bills, and real climate benefits without leaving so many important members of our community on the losing side of the ledger.” The oil and gas industry has a different take on the election results. Mike Sommers, chief executive of the American Petroleum Institute, said the affordability message was unmistakable and called the permitting bill the place for bipartisan cooperation to start. The White House said Trump remained committed to reliable, affordable and secure energy. However, the incoming class of Democrats is not of one mind. U.S. Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas promised to protect oil and gas jobs. Rep.-elect Cait Conley (D-N.Y.) framed climate change as a “national security crisis” and called for federal investment in solar, wind and geothermal power and a return to the Paris climate agreement. Rep.-elect Will Lawrence, a 36-year-old co-founder of the climate advocacy group Sunrise Movement who won a swing seat in Michigan, campaigned for state and federal moratoriums on hyperscale data centers — and, as Grist reported , has moved away from the Green New Deal’s massive build-out toward the politics of community control over projects and clean energy. The states: Six new trifectas The most immediate changes are expected where Democrats won the governor’s office and both legislative chambers: Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. The party also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. Pennsylvania has the biggest runway. Democrats flipped the state Senate to cement the first trifecta since 1993, and lawmakers plan to pass long-stalled bills streamlining community solar, warehouse solar and battery storage while barring local governments from banning renewable projects. Gov. Josh Shapiro, who has presidential aspirations, has also proposed a carbon cap-and-trade program, which sets a hard cap on emissions, similar to what California and other states have on the books. Related: Starbucks Gets a Tax Break: Families Pick Up the Tab In Michigan and Minnesota, restored trifectas are likely to protect laws requiring 100% clean electricity by 2040 from repeal and open the door to grid modernization bills. In Arizona and Wisconsin, new majorities could pursue the renewable standards and decarbonization targets that Republican legislatures blocked for years. Utility regulators are shifting too. Democrats won both open seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission for a 3-2 majority, their first majority in decades, and new appointments in Michigan and Arizona are expected to bring tougher scrutiny of utility spending on fossil fuels. Michigan voters went further, approving a measure that bars state-regulated utilities such as DTE Energy from contributing to the campaigns of officials who oversee them. The bill was backed by U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed. A separate measure to replace DTE Energy with a public utility was narrowly defeated. Local: The data center revolt Closer to home, the story was almost entirely data centers. Voters in 10 states decided 41 local measures, 21 of them in Ohio, and 32 with reported results favoring limits. Pataskala and Granville, Ohio, approved bans on facilities above 25 megawatts with 74% and 82% of the vote. Newly elected local officials in states such as in Pennsylvania and Virginia campaigned on the same promise — reining in data centers. They are expected to tighten zoning, require new facilities to procure their own renewable power and keep utilities from passing grid upgrade costs on to residential ratepayers. Not every local measure said no. Voters in Eugene, Oregon, approved a Clean Energy Fund that places a 2% license fee on large retailers such as Amazon and Walmart to pay for renewable energy and job training. It is expected to raise at least $15 million a year by 2030 and was modeled on Portland’s 2018 fund, which has invested $1.7 billion. Related: Trump's Coal Revival Is Raising Electric Bills—and Voters Are Fighting Back The local votes set up the next fight. Pennsylvania Democrats want to stop towns from banning solar farms even as towns across the Midwest vote to ban data centers — and legislatures weighing statewide rules will have to decide whether to codify those bans or override them. Garin, the Democratic pollster, said the politics favored his side. Each of those issues, he said, “gave Democrats the high ground in the energy debate, and I think that that will continue to be the case as we move from elections into legislating and policymaking.” Capital & Main
